DATE:  APRIL 17, 2024

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  PARKS AND RECREATION DEPARTMENT

DISTRICT:  ALL

SUBJECT:  APPROVE AGREEMENT WITH PFD MANAGEMENT, INC. TO
  PROVIDE CONCESSION SERVICES AT DRYTOWN WATER PARK,
  FOR REVENUES OF $42,000 ANNUALLY FOR A TERM OF THREE
  YEARS WITH THE OPTION TO EXTEND TWO ONE-YEAR TERMS

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-8766 with PFD Management, Inc. to provide
  concession services at DryTown Water Park for revenues of $42,000 annually for
  a term of three years with the option to extend two one-year terms; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute Agreement No. A-8766
  with PFD Management, Inc., including minimal and/or non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND

DryTown Water Park opened in 2006, and park concession services have been
operated by a contractor since 2008. Due to the water park's seasonal nature,
contracting concession personnel is cost-effective and allows for greater purchasing
power, industry expertise and knowledge, assurance of quality control, and compliance.

Concession services include full-service food and beverage offerings, which include
freshly-prepared hot meals, convenience, and snack items. The concessionaire
operates two park food service locations and proposes introducing mobile service items
in the upcoming season. Our current concession agreement with PFD Management,
Inc. expired on March 31, 2024, and the park is scheduled to open on May 24, 2024.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Approve Agreement No. A-8766 with PFD Management, Inc.
April 17, 2024
Page 2

DISCUSSION

PFD Management, Inc. has provided DryTown Water Park concession services from
2018 to 2023. Park visitors often express high satisfaction regarding the food quality, the
diversity of the menu offerings, and the generous portion sizes available. PFD
Management, Inc. has also continued to expand healthy menu options and offers a variety
of items from different cuisines.

The City released a Request for Proposal (RFP) No. 23-001-4440 for Concession
Services for DryTown Water Park on October 26, 2023. Notifications were released
through PlanetBids and sent to 35 food service vendors. The City received one complete
proposal and one incomplete proposal.

Staff received and evaluated PFD Management, Inc.’s proposal and determined it to
meet all requirements outlined in the RFP. Proposal details include group pricing,
affordable price points, expanded food distribution areas, and a streamlined menu to
expedite service. Our past experience with PFD Management, Inc. has demonstrated
excellent quality control, trustworthy business practices, and a product that park guests
enjoy. It is recommended that Agreement No. A-8766 be awarded to PFD Management,
Inc. The contract term will be for three years, from April 22, 2024 through April 21, 2027
with the option to extend two additional one-year terms.

FISCAL IMPACT

$42,000 annually in revenue. Terms of the agreement include compensation to the City
in accordance with the below schedule:

 Year  Percent of Sales
 Year One of the Agreement  13% of Gross Sales Provided to the City
 Year Two of the Agreement  14% of Gross Sales Provided to the City
 Year Three of the Agreement  15% of Gross Sales Provided to the City

The City does not hire concession services; historically, the vendor manages sales and
compensates the City for a portion of sales. Over the last three fiscal years, in
partnership with PFD Management, Inc., the City has received an average of $42,000
annually in revenue. This is used to offset the costs of utilities, kitchen maintenance, and
the upkeep of appliances in the concession stands. The previous split was 10% of gross
sales, and the current agreement proposes an increase to 13% with an annual escalator.
PFD's menu pricing is positioned below that of comparable water and theme parks. This
is highlighted by the average per capita spending on food and beverages of $5.25 per
patron in recent years, below the industry average of $11.09.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Approve Agreement No. A-8766 with PFD Management, Inc.
April 17, 2024
Page 3

  Agreement No.A-8766
  Between the City of Palmdale andPFD Management
  Inc

 THIS CONTRACT FOR SERVICES is made and entered into by and between the
 City of Palmdale a public body corporate and politic, (hereinafter called “CITY”),
 and PFD MANAGEMENT INC.(hereinafter called “CONCESSIONAIRE”) for
 concession services at DryTown Water Park, located at 3850-B East Avenue S in
 Palmdale, California. This Contract shall become effective on the date of the last
 signatory.

  RECITALS
WHEREAS, CONCESSIONAIRE represents that CONCESSIONAIRE has the
expertise and qualifications to perform the services described in this contract.
NOW THEREFORE, CITY and CONCESSIONAIRE, in consideration of the mutual
covenants hereinafter set forth, agree as follows:

 1. TERM OF AGREEMENT

 The term of this agreement is Three 3 Years. CITY has the option of extending the
 agreement for two (2) additional one (1) year terms. CITY, through its City
 Manager, shall provide written notice to CONCESSIONAIRE of its intent to extend
 the agreement at least sixty (60) days prior to the end of the initial term.

 2. SCOPE OF SERVICE AND GENERAL PROVISIONS

 CONCESSIONAIRE shall provide directly to CITY concessionaire services for
 which the CITY cannot offer at its facility. Specifically, CONCESSIONAIRE shall
 offer for sale all meals, food, and non-alcoholic beverages, as specified in RFP 23-
 001-4440 Food Services for DryTown Water Park and the food and beverage list
 attached as Exhibit A, and hereby incorporated by reference, at DryTown Water
 Park.

 3. COMPENSATION AND PAYMENT SCHEDULE

  3.1 CONCESSIONAIRE can negotiate its own rates and has negotiated
  with CITY the following rate structure:
  YEAR 1 –13% out of gross sales
  YEAR 2 - 14% out of gross sales
  YEAR 3 - 15% out of gross sales

  3.2 CONCESSIONAIRE will collect and deposit all revenues received and,
  issue payments to CITY. CONCESSIONAIRE shall issue payment on,
  or before, the due 10th day of each month. A late fee of 5% per month
  will be assessed to any payment not received by the 10th day of the

  Concord - Document ID: 02wEez9Id2r7D1KUC5DCL5  1-13
   month.
  3.3 CONCESSIONAIRE will provide CITY, at the time of payment, daily
  and weekly gross sales reports and individual item sales reports (if
  applicable) from all concession points of sale at DryTown Water Park.

  3.4 The failure of the CONCESSIONAIRE to make a timely compensation
  payment will be considered a material breach of this agreement.
  3.5 PFD Management will also donate $500.00 each semester for
  scholarship through our scholarship program to DryTown Water Park
  staff who are enrolled in high school or college.

4. HOURS OF OPERATION

 CONCESSIONAIRE is free to control the manner and method by which it
 provides concessionaire services to CITY and can set its own hours and location
 of work. CONCESSIONAIRE, in an effort to maximize its sales, requests to
 provide concessions during all operating hours of DryTown Water Park and
 during any private parties, park buy-outs, and other events. CITY agrees to this
 request.

5. USE OF EQUIPMENT AND FACILITIES

  5.1 CONCESSIONAIRE provides its own tools, vehicles, and equipment to
  perform these services to CITY, however, it is authorized to use all
  concession facilities, including Dusty’s Grill and all equipment located
  in Dusty’s Grill.

  5.2 CONCESSIONAIRE agrees to maintain any and all concession
  facilities and equipment in good order and repair, at levels and in
  manners satisfactory to CITY.

  5.3 CONCESSIONAIRE, at its own expense, may purchase additional
  equipment as needed to prepare, store, or serve food and beverage
  items. CONCESSIONAIRE must first obtain written approval from
  CITY to make any major alterations to the set-up of Dusty’s Grill (i.e.
  installation of new equipment).

  5.4 CONCESSIONAIRE, at its own expense, shall provide and maintain in
  operation point of sale (POS) equipment necessary for the successful
  and efficient operation of all concession facilities. Equipment must be
  capable of processing credit card transactions.

6. INVENTORY

  6.1 Prior to opening day of each operating season, CITY personnel and
  CONCESSIONAIRE will conduct an inventory of all equipment and
  agree upon the equipment contained in Dusty’s Grill. At the conclusion
  of each operating season, CITY personnel and CONCESSIONAIRE
  will conduct a final inventory of all equipment contained in Dusty’s
  Grill. CONCESSIONAIRE will be responsible for replacement costs of

  Concord - Document ID: 02wEez9Id2r7D1KUC5DCL5  2-13
   any missing equipment or damage to any CITY equipment caused by
  the acts or omissions of CONCESSIONAIRE or any of its employees,
  officers, agents, or contractors.

  6.2 At the conclusion of each Operating Season, CONCESSIONAIRE
  shall return Dusty’s Grill to its clean, pre-use condition to CITY’S
  satisfaction.  CITY  will  charge  CONCESSIONAIRE,  and
  CONCESSIONAIRE agrees to pay for any expense incurred in
  cleaning or returning Dusty’s Grill to its clean, pre-use condition.

7. CONCESSIONAIRE STAFF AND CUSTOMER SERVICE

  7.1 CONCESSIONAIRE shall provide and supervise sufficiently trained
  employees to render good service and perform necessary
  maintenance in Dusty’s Grill and other concession points of sale.

  7.2 CONCESSIONAIRE agrees that it shall not hire or retain any
  employee who is required to register under Penal Code Section 290,
  or who has been convicted of any crime of violence, or crime involving
  theft, or any felony, within the ten (10) previous years.

  7.3 CONCESSIONAIRE shall furnish courteous, efficient, and quality
  service to meet the reasonable demands of CITY, and all DryTown
  Water Park customers. CONCESSIONAIRE shall control, and is
  responsible for, the conduct, demeanor, and appearance of its officers,
  agents, employees, representatives, guests, contractors, and others
  while doing business as provided herein.

8. CITY STAFF

  8.1 CITY will support CONCESSIONAIRE and provide courteous and
  professional assistance when needed. CITY will communicate with
  CONCESSIONAIRE regarding birthday parties, group events, after-
  hour events, and to review Dusty’s Grill operations.

  8.2 CITY will attempt to address any issues presented to CITY regarding
  Dusty’s Grill and work with CONCESSIONAIRE to resolve issues as
  quickly as possible.

9. COMPLIANCE WITH LAW

  9.1 CONCESSIONAIRE shall comply with all state and federal laws,
  including but not limited to, the requirement to hire only those persons
  authorized by federal law to work in the United States. If
  CONCESSIONAIRE uses any subcontractors to complete this Contract,
  this same requirement shall be included in all subcontracts and strictly
  enforced by CONCESSIONAIRE.
  9.2 CONCESSIONAIRE agrees to abide by all DryTown Water Park
  general rules and regulations. CITY will provide CONCESSIONAIRE a
  copy of all rules and regulations governing DryTown Water Park.

  Concord - Document ID: 02wEez9Id2r7D1KUC5DCL5  3-13
   9.3 The law of the state of California shall govern this Contract. The venue
  of any legal action, either formal or informal, shall be the County of Los
  Angeles.

10. NON-DISCRIMINATION AND EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY

  10.1 In performance of this Contract, CONCESSIONAIRE shall not
  discriminate against any employee, subcontractor, or applicant for
  employment because of sex, color, race, religion, ancestry, national
  origin, disability, medical condition including the medical condition of
  Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) or any condition
  related thereto, marital status, sexual orientation, age, gender, gender
  identity, gender expression, genetic information, or military and
  veteran status. CONCESSIONAIRE will take affirmative action to ensure
  that applicants are employed, and that employees are treated during
  employment, without regard to their sex, color, race, religion, ancestry,
  national origin, disability, medical condition including the medical
  condition of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) or any
  condition related thereto, marital status, sexual orientation, age,
  gender, gender identity, gender expression, genetic information, or
  military and veteran status . Affirmative action relating to employment
  shall include, but not be limited to the following: employment,
  upgrading, demotion or transfer; recruitment; layoff or termination;
  rates of pay or other forms of compensation; and selection for training,
  including apprenticeship.

  10.2 The provisions of subsection 10.1 above shall be included in all
  solicitations or advertisements placed by or on behalf of
  CONCESSIONAIRE for personnel to perform any services under this
  Contract. CITY shall have access to all documents, data and records
  of CONCESSIONAIRE and its subcontractors for purposes of
  determining compliance with the equal employment opportunity and
  non-discrimination provisions of this Section, and all applicable
  provisions of Executive Order No. 11246 which is incorporated herein
  by this reference. A copy of Executive Order No. 11246 is available for
  inspection at, and on file with, the Palmdale City Clerk’s Office.

11. MENU AND PRICING

  11.1 CONCESSIONAIRE proposes to provide the menu identified in Exhibit
  A, A-1, A-2, A-3, A-4, A-5, A-6, A-7, & A-8.

12. VENDORS/ SUPPLIES

  12.1 CONCESSIONAIRE shall be responsible for selecting their own food
  and supplies vendors. All vendors shall be reputable and be selected
  not only because of price but also for food quality and overall customer
  service.

  Concord - Document ID: 02wEez9Id2r7D1KUC5DCL5  4-13
   12.2 CONCESSIONAIRE, at its own expense, shall always carry in stock
  adequate food, beverages, and supplies items, as is customary in
  similar establishments, to render good service to patrons of DryTown
  Water Park. CONCESSIONAIRE shall be responsible for the
  procurement of all stock and other necessary materials at no cost to
  CITY. All food, beverages, and refreshments sold or kept for sale by
  the CONCESSIONAIRE, shall be first class in quality, wholesome and
  pure, and shall conform to all federal, state, and local food laws,
  ordinances, and regulations in all respects. No imitation, adulterated,
  misbranded, or impure articles shall be sold or kept for sale by the
  CONCESSIONAIRE. All merchandise kept on hand by
  CONCESSIONAIRE shall be stored and handled with due regard for
  sanitation and in compliance with all health regulations.

  12.3 Due to exclusivity contracts already in place, CONCESSIONAIRE shall
  comply with CITY exclusive bottling agreements. CONCESSIONAIRE
  shall purchase, pay for, and serve only products sold by CITY
  exclusive bottling company.

13. NONEXCLUSIVE CONTRACT

  It is agreed by the parties hereto that this Agreement is not an exclusive
  contract for such services between the CITY and CONCESSIONAIRE. CITY
  may, at its sole option, contract with other entities for concessions services
  providing products not in direct competition with items sold by
  CONCESSIONAIRE.

14. INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR

  CONCESSIONAIRE is customarily engaged in an independently established
  business providing catering and concessionaire services. CONCESSIONAIRE
  maintains a business location that is separate from DryTown Water Park or any
  other CITY facility. CONCESSIONAIRE advertises and holds itself out to the
  public as available to provide the same or similar services as provided in this
  Agreement, and contracts with other businesses to provide these services.
  CONCESSIONAIRE maintains a clientele without restrictions from CITY.
  CONCESSIONAIRE is required to have a business license to operate in the city
  of Palmdale and has obtained the required business license.
  CONCESSIONAIRE, in performing concession services, shall act as an
  independent contractor and shall have control of its work and the manner in
  which it is performed. CONCESSIONAIRE is not an agent or employee of CITY
  and is not entitled to any benefits provided by CITY to its employees.

15. UTILITIES AND FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEMS

  15.1 CITY shall pay the reasonable costs of providing water, gas, trash,
  telephone, electricity, and data lines. CONCESSIONAIRE shall pay all
  credit card fees related to conducting business at DryTown Water
  Park.

  Concord - Document ID: 02wEez9Id2r7D1KUC5DCL5  5-13
   15.2 CITY shall pay for the annual inspection to comply with UL 300 Fire
  Marshall Code and the inspection of all fire extinguishers.

16. SIGNS AND ADVERTISEMENTS

  CONCESSIONAIRE shall not erect, install, operate nor cause or permit to be
  erected, installed, or operated in or upon Dusty’s Grill or DryTown Water Park,
  any sign or other similar advertising device without having first obtained prior
  written consent from CITY. CONCESSIONAIRE, at its own expense, shall
  install a new menu board that shall be mutually agreed upon by
  CONCESSIONAIRE and CITY. Any such sign or similar advertising device
  erected, installed, or operated during the term of this Agreement must be
  removed, at the sole cost of CONCESSIONAIRE, immediately upon termination
  or expiration of this Agreement. CONCESSIONAIRE will not advertise offsite
  businesses without prior, written approval of CITY.

17. CLEANLINESS

  17.1 Prior to opening Dusty’s Grill, CONCESSIONAIRE will conduct an

  THE AMOUNT OF THE AGREEMENT BY $680,300 FOR A TOTAL

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Second Amendment No. A-7866 with Pacific West Sound, Inc. to
  provide audio production and equipment services for the Palmdale Amphitheater
  to increase the amount of the agreement by $680,300, for a total amount not-to-
  exceed $946,500 for a three-year term through June 30, 2025, with the option to
  extend two additional one-year terms; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute Second Amendment
  Agreement No. A-7866 with Pacific West Sound, Inc., including minimal and/or
  non-substantial changes; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to exercise the option to extend two
  additional one-year terms.

BACKGROUND

The Palmdale Amphitheater hosts a variety of live headliner concerts and community
events requiring top-tier audio production services and equipment. The venue does not
have permanently installed audio production equipment. Therefore, all associated stage
audio equipment and operation services are contracted to meet artist performance
agreements.

DISCUSSION

Pacific West Sound, Inc. has been providing audio production and equipment services
at the Palmdale Amphitheater since June 2022, under Agreement No. A-7866, which
expires on June 30, 2025 with the option to extend two additional one-year terms. The
vendor has provided exceptional service and has successfully met complicated artist
performance requirements.

Increased service demands require for the agreement amount to be augmented to cover
the expanded two-day Kaleidoscope Art and Music Festival, July 4th Celebration,
additional concert performance dates, rental of stage LED walls for select events, rental
of improved hearing-impaired listening devices, additional artist-specific equipment, and
production labor. The approval of Second Amendment to Agreement No. A-7866 will
increase the contract by an additional $680,300. This amount will fund services to
complete the three-year term and includes additional funds for two additional one-year
options to extend.

(Events and Culture, Kaleidoscope) for fiscal year 2023-2024. Funding for services in
fiscal years 24/25 through 26/27 will be evaluated and approved as part of the annual
budget adoption process.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve the third amendment to Agreement No. A-7819 with Bradley, Gmelich &
  Wellerstein, LLP for legal services to increase the agreement amount by $400,000,
  for a total not to exceed amount of $1,390,000 for the remainder of the term
  through February 2025; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the third amendment to
  Agreement No. A-7819 with Bradley, Gmelich & Wellerstein, LLP, including
  minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

Bradley, Gmelich & Wellerstein, LLP (BGW) has competently provided legal services to
the City for over a decade. The firm provides legal services for personal injury, property
damage, and employment law defense. The budgeted contract amount has been
depleted and must now be augmented to allow them to continue providing services.

DISCUSSION

In 2022, the City Council approved an agreement between the City and BGW to provide
legal services, including cross-claims, counter-claims, summary judgments, motions,
discovery proceedings, trials, and post-trial and appellate work. It is noted that Harper

until 2025.

SUBJECT:  SUMMARY OF THE  2023  ANNUAL  HOUSING  ELEMENT
  PROGRESS REPORT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Receive the summary of the 2023 Annual Housing Element Progress Report; and,

  2. Direct staff to file the report with the California Department of Housing and
  Community Development (HCD).

BACKGROUND

Government Code Section 65400 requires that all California cities provide an Annual
Housing Element Progress Report to the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research
(OPR) and the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).
The intent of the statute is to describe the City’s progress in meeting its share of the
Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). Also, by filing this report with OPR and
HCD, the City may be eligible for future housing grants.

DISCUSSION

A total of 6,640 units were allocated to the City of Palmdale during the 6th cycle RHNA
allocation plan, which covers the planning period October 2021 through October 2029.
These units are distributed by affordability level, and the Housing Element of the General
Plan must identify how the City plans to accommodate them. The City is required to
designate land for housing to ensure that there is enough residentially designated land to
meet its RHNA allocation. However, it is not required to ensure units are built. The City is
required to report on the progress of housing development in the form of the Annual
Housing Element Progress Report.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE THE SECOND AMENDMENT TO AGREEMENT WITH
  RETAIL STRATEGIES, LLC FOR RETAIL ATTRACTION AND
  RECRUITMENT SERVICES TO INCREASE THE AMOUNT OF THE
  AGREEMENT BY $45,000, FOR A TOTAL NOT TO EXCEED AMOUNT
  OF $135,000 AND EXTEND THE AGREEMENT TERM BY ONE YEAR
  TO APRIL 1, 2025

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve the second amendment to Agreement No. A-7873 with Retail Strategies,
  LLC, for retail attraction and recruitment services to increase the amount of the
  agreement by $45,000, for a not to exceed amount of $135,000 and extend
  agreement term by one year to April 1, 2025; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager, or her designee, to execute the second amendment
  to Agreement No. A-7873 with Retail Strategies, LLC, including minimal and/or
  non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

In February 2022, the City released a Request for Proposals (RFP) for retail attraction
and recruitment services. This initiative aimed to solicit competitive proposals from firms
with a strong understanding of retail dynamics and well-established relationships with
retailer and commercial broker communities who could navigate the City's economic
environment. After reviewing the proposals, the City selected and executed Agreement
No. A-7873 with Retail Strategies, LLC. The initial agreement was $45,000 per year for a
two-year term, for a not to exceed amount of $90,000.

In March 2023, the City Council approved a First Amendment to the Agreement clarifying
that the services provided in the scope of work aligned with the American Rescue Plan
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Amendment to Agreement with Retail Strategies, LLC
April 17, 2024
Page 2

Act's (ARPA) goals and requirements. No other amendments were made to the
agreement.

Since their selection in 2022, Staff has worked with Retail Strategies to develop data and
market analysis, evaluate commercial properties for potential development, and execute
targeted outreach efforts. In addition to these efforts, Retail Strategies creates marketing
brochures showcasing various commercial sites to use with potential investors and
retailers. Retail Strategies also attended various retail shows on behalf of the City,
facilitated business meetings at the annual International Council of Shopping Centers
(ICSC) trade show, and provided meeting space at the event for the City to utilize. This
collaborative approach has provided invaluable technical assistance to businesses,
ensuring a multifaceted strategy to enhance the City’s retail sector.

DISCUSSION

The second amendment extends the agreement term for one additional year through April
1, 2025, and augments the agreement amount to allow Retail Strategies to continue
providing essential retail recruitment services that align with and actively promote the
City's long-term economic development goals. The continuation of this partnership is
expected to yield ongoing benefits by attracting diverse retail options, improving local
employment opportunities, and increasing the City's tax base.

FISCAL IMPACT

$45,000; funds for the second amendment to Agreement No. A-7873 are allocated under
ARPA. The account has $100,000 for retail consulting, of which $45,000 will be used to
pay for the work completed during the extended term of this agreement.

BACKGROUND

In 2014, the City secured the refinancing of previously issued debt with a lease of
property consisting of Marie Kerr Park and Dry Town Water Park (2014 Lease). Due to
the reduction in the outstanding balance of the 2014 Lease, the City can release Marie
Kerr Park from the 2014 Lease, leaving it secured only by Dry Town Water Park until its
final maturity in September 2032.

DISCUSSION

The City issued Certificates of Participation in 2002 (2002 COPs) to finance various
improvements, including Dry Town Water Park and improvements to Marie Kerr Park
and Avenue S. In 2014, the City refinanced a portion of the 2002 COPs and secured the
payments due with a lease of property consisting of Marie Kerr Park and Dry Town
Water Park.

The original 2014 Lease was issued for $25.9 million. The current balance is $15.86
million. Due to the reduction in the outstanding balance, Marie Kerr Park can be released
from the 2014 Lease, leaving only Dry Town Water Park as security for the lease
payments. The lease payments will be paid in full by September 2032 and are currently
paid from Park Assessment Funds.

Once Marie Kerr Park is released from the 2014 lease, it can be used to secure financing
for other City leases in the future.

The 2014 Lease was entered into between the City and the Palmdale Financing
Authority (Authority). Payments due to the Authority under the 2014 Lease were then
assigned to the lender, TPB Investments (TPB). TPB has been succeeded by Western
Alliance Business Trust (Western Alliance), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Western
Alliance Bank. To accomplish this, the Bank has agreed to the release of Marie Kerr
Park and the amendment of the existing financing documents.

Resolutions of the City and the Authority presented to the City Council and the Board of
Directors approve the form of the following documents, which remove Marie Kerr Park
from the description of the leased property:

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2024-031, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE TO ESTABLISH A
  VEHICLE MILES TRAVELED (VMT) PROGRAM WHICH INCLUDES
  VMT THRESHOLDS, VMT ANALYSIS REQUIREMENTS AND
  PROGRAM; AND ESTABLISHES TWO NEW CITY FEES: A VMT
  ANALYSIS FEE AND A VMT IMPACT FEE

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Hold a public hearing to accept public testimony and adopt Resolution No. CC
  2024-031; and,

  2. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-031, which recommends a four percent (4%) VMT
  threshold, analysis requirement and mitigation program, including a new VMT
  Analysis Fee and a VMT Impact Fee of $261 as provided for in the City of Palmdale
  SB 743 VMT Implementation Guidelines.

BACKGROUND

SB 743, signed into law by California Governor Jerry Brown in 2013, updated how
transportation impacts were measured in California for new development projects,
ensuring they were built to allow Californians more options to drive less. However, SB
743 effectively resulted in automobile delay, as measured by the “level of service” (LOS),
and no longer constitutes a significant environmental effect under the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). (Pub. Resources Code, § 21099(b)(2)). This change
in the analysis of transportation impacts went into effect when the CEQA Guidelines were
updated to make the revisions called for in SB 743 and were certified by the Natural
Resources Agency in December 2018.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2024-031
April 17, 2024
Page 2

The Governor’s Office of Planning and Research (OPR) selected VMT as the principal
measure to replace LOS for determining significant transportation impacts. VMT
measures total vehicular travel that accounts for the number and length of vehicle trips.
OPR selected VMT in part because jurisdictions are already familiar with this metric. VMT
is used in CEQA to study other potential impacts such as greenhouse gases (GHG), air
quality, and energy impacts and is used in planning for regional Sustainable Communities
Strategies (SCS).

To date, projects across the State identified as having a significant transportation project
have relied heavily on Transportation Demand Measures (TDMs) if they could not mitigate
with on-site solutions. While TDMs can be effective, particularly in highly urbanized areas,
they are generally less effective in suburban and rural contexts. TDMs can also be
challenging from the standpoint of mitigation monitoring and can result in the requirement
that a project manage and pay for them in perpetuity. These limitations have led
jurisdictions to consider programmatic approaches and TDMs for VMT mitigation.

DISCUSSION

The City has relied on the Los Angeles County Public Works Transportation Impact
Analysis Guidelines, dated July 23, 2020, for SB 743 analysis. To better reflect the unique
character and needs of the City of Palmdale, new implementation guidelines have been
prepared and are recommended for adoption. The proposed implementation guidelines
include thresholds and analysis requirements for land use and transportation
improvement projects. The implementation guidelines also include a VMT mitigation
program to meet the needs of projects that require solutions beyond those directly
available to a project or that can be achieved through TDMs.

The proposed program allows for a project to use site-specific mitigation solutions, TDMs,

Staff will manage a new VMT mitigation program and associated reporting. Other costs
may be incurred by projects that participate in the proposed VMT mitigation program to
mitigate a significant transportation impact.

   SB 743 VMT Implementation Guidelines for the City of Palmdale

Background
In 2013, SB 743 was signed into law by California Governor Jerry Brown with a goal of reducing Greenhouse
Gas (GHG) emissions, promoting the development of infill land use projects and multimodal transportation
networks, and to promote a diversity of land uses within developments. One significant outcome resulting
from this statute is that automobile delay, as measured by “level of service” (LOS) and other similar metrics,
generally no longer constitutes a significant environmental effect under the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA). (Pub. Resources Code, § 21099(b)(2)). This change in the analysis of transportation
impacts went into effect when the CEQA Guidelines were updated to make the revisions called for in SB
743 and were certified by the Natural Resources Agency in December, 2018.
The Governor’s Office of Planning and Research (OPR) selected Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) as the
principal measure to replace LOS for determining significant transportation impacts. VMT is a measure of
total vehicular travel that accounts for the number of vehicle trips and the length of those trips. OPR
selected VMT, in part, because jurisdictions are already familiar with this metric. VMT is already used in
CEQA to study other potential impacts such as GHG, air quality, and energy impacts and is used in planning
for regional Sustainable Communities Strategies (SCS). As of July 1, 2020, agencies analyzing the
transportation impacts of new projects must look at VMT as a metric known as vehicle miles traveled (VMT)
instead of LOS.
VMT also allows for an analysis of a project’s impact throughout the jurisdiction rather than only in the
vicinity of the proposed project allowing for a better understanding of the full extent of a project’s
transportation-related impact.

Use of this Document
This document has been developed to serve both as the basis of SB 743 implementation and VMT analysis
within the City. While this document includes footnotes and references to other documents, the use of this
document does not require the reader to reference the footnotes unless they are interested in
understanding the technical basis of elements of this document’s preparation. The analysis guidelines are
separated into two distinct approaches, those that relate to land use projects and those that relate to
transportation improvement projects. If a project includes both land use and transportation improvement
elements, analysis would be required to be carried out for both. Projects not subject to CEQA are not
required to follow these guidelines. This includes projects that are reviewed under existing ministerial or
administrative processes, site plan review, and other actions that do not require environmental review.

Land Use Projects
The approach included within this document for identifying transportation impacts under CEQA for land-
use projects, in part, aligns with guidance provided within the OPR Technical Advisory on Evaluating
Transportation Impacts in CEQA (2018).
While the OPR guidance related to SB 743 has been a helpful introduction to using VMT to evaluate
projects, it does not provide a complete solution. There are a multitude of complex practical issues that are
not addressed by the OPR guidance. OPR Guidance does not specifically address land uses beyond
residential, office, and retail, and it provides latitude on some elements of implementation. In response to
this, a specific series of analytical steps for SB 743 project evaluation have been developed to clarify
requirements and reduce potential confusion. Exhibit 1 provides a graphical representation of this
analytical process.

Step 1: Evaluate Land Use Type
During the initial step, the land use projects will need to be evaluated for the following considerations:
  ▪  Land use type. For the purposes of analysis, the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) land use
  codes serve as the basis of land use definitions. Although it is recognized that VMT evaluation tools
  and methodologies are typically not fully sensitive to some of the distinctions between some ITE
  categories, the use of ITE land use codes is useful for maintaining consistency across analyses,
  determining trip generation for other planning level tools, and maintaining a common
  understanding of trip making characteristics amongst transportation professionals. The ITE land
  use code is also used as an input into the City’s VMT analysis tool.
  ▪  Mixed Use. If there are multiple distinct land uses within the project (residential, office, retail, etc.),
  they will be required to be analyzed separately unless they are determined to be insignificant to
  the total VMT. Mixed use projects are permitted to account for internal capture which depending
  on the methodology may require a distinct approach not covered in this documentation.
  ▪  Redevelopment projects. As described under the Non-Significant Screening Criteria section,
  redevelopment projects which have lower VMT than the existing on-site use can be determined to
  have a non-significant impact.

Step 2: Screen for Non-Significant Transportation Impact
The purpose of this step is to determine if a presumption of a non-significant transportation impact can be
made on the facts of the project. The guidance in this section is primarily intended to avoid unnecessary
analysis and findings that would be inconsistent with the City’s implementation of SB 743. A detailed CEQA
transportation analysis will not be required for land use elements of a project that meet the screening
criteria shown in Exhibit 2. If a project is mixed use in nature, only those elements of the project that do
not comply with the elements in Exhibit 2 would require further evaluation to determine transportation
significance for CEQA purposes.

Step 3: Significance Threshold and Methodology
The purpose of this step is to determine the threshold of significance for application to a land use project.
Significance thresholds are based on land use type, broadly categorized as efficiency and net change
metrics. Efficiency metrics include VMT/capita and work VMT/employee11. As shown in Exhibit 1, projects
involving residential and office land uses would be evaluated using efficiency metrics; whereas, projects
that include a significant customer/user base, such as retail and other commercial uses, would be evaluated
based on the net change in regional VMT based on customer/user trips. Exhibit 3 provides a few examples
of the variety of uses that have similar characteristics for using Efficiency or Net Change metrics.
For projects with a significant customer/user base, it is typically appropriate to separate employee trip
characteristics from the customer base trip characteristics, unless the customer base is minimal in nature.
Under these circumstances, it is most appropriate to evaluate the total of the delta in regional VMT
resulting from the customer base plus the delta of VMT resulting from employees based on the following
formula:
  (number of employees) x (estimated VMT/employee – threshold VMT/employee)

VMT Thresholds of Significance
OPR recommends a 15-percent VMT reduction relative to existing development may be a reasonable
threshold. While OPR’s Technical Advisory is not binding on public agencies, CEQA allows lead agencies to
“consider thresholds of significance…recommended by other public agencies, provided the decision to
adopt those thresholds is supported by substantial evidence.”12
According to OPR, achieving 15-percent lower per capita (for residential development) or per employee
(for employment-based development) VMT compared with VMT resulting from existing development is
both generally achievable and is supported by evidence that connects this level of reduction to the State’s
emissions goals.13 The thresholds of significance recommended by OPR, as they relate to the City of

VMT Analysis Tool
The City of Palmdale has developed a VMT analysis tool for use in SB 743 land use project analysis. The
purpose of the tool is to calculate VMT for a land use project without the use of the City’s General Plan
travel demand model. As with any sketch planning tool, there are distinct limitations in terms of its
application including limits on the type and size of development that the tool can be applied to. Generally
speaking, it is not appropriate that the tool be applied to land use projects that have greater than 2,500
total trips per day unless the City has made a determination that it is an appropriate application. Note that
it is anticipated that the tool will continue to evolve in response to data and methodological changes and
as such, it is important that the most current version of the tool be utilized. Broadly, the tool provides the
following information:
  ▪  Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation
  ▪  VMT Threshold Analysis
  ▪  Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Estimation
  ▪  Transportation Demand Management (TDM) Evaluation
  ▪  Potential VMT Mitigation Bank Costs

Step 4: VMT Analysis
Prior to undertaking a VMT analysis for a proposed project, a scope of work that is compliant with the City
of Palmdale’s requirements should be prepared and submitted for approval. Given the potential
complexities of some uses, particularly those not identified as residential, retail, or other primary
employment uses such as office or industrial, an agreement with the City regarding the threshold and
methodology is important to avoid completing an analysis that is not compliant with CEQA and the City of
Palmdale’s standards.
Relevant documentation should be provided that includes enough detail that assumptions are clearly
understandable and methods that can be replicated. In addition, the results of the VMT analysis for the
proposed project should be provided in the relevant documentation.

Step 5: Mitigation Measures
If a significant transportation impact is identified, the City of Palmdale, as the lead agency, will require that
mitigation or alternatives be considered. CEQA requires that the mitigation measures or alternatives are
included in the project’s environmental assessment analysis. OPR has provided a list of potential measures
to reduce VMT but CEQA allows for a lead agency, such as the City of Palmdale, discretion in the selection
of mitigation measures.
The type and size of the project will determine the most appropriate mitigation strategies for VMT impacts.
For large projects such as general plans or specific plans, VMT mitigations should concentrate on the
project’s density and land use mix, site design, regional policies, and availability of transit, bicycle, and
pedestrian facilities. For smaller projects such as an individual development project, VMT mitigations will
typically require the preparation of a transportation demand management (TDM) program. A TDM program
is a combination of strategies to reduce VMT. The program is created by an applicant for their land use
project based on a list of strategies agreed to with the City of Palmdale.
The City of Palmdale has developed a list of potential TDM strategies appropriate for the City and what
magnitude of VMT reduction could be achieved. The TDM options are based on those identified in by the
California Air Pollution Control Officers Association (CAPCOA) recommendations as provided in the 2021
publication Handbook for Analyzing Greenhouse Gas Emission Reductions, Assessing Climate Vulnerabilities,
and Advancing Health and Equity. The City of Palmdale’s VMT analysis tool includes TDM options and the
ability to calculate the total VMT reduction based on a combination of the TDMs selected and their relative
efficacy at reducing the project’s VMT.
The City of Palmdale has also established a VMT Banking Mitigation Program to address mitigation needs.
Discussion on this program is provided in the next section.

Step 6: Monitoring Mitigation
As required by CEQA, the City of Palmdale will require ongoing mitigation monitoring and reporting when
mitigation measures are adopted as part of an approved project. The specifics of this will be developed on
a project-by-project basis. As an example, the City may require the determination of a “trip cap” (the
number of vehicle trips entering/existing the site that would correspond with the threshold VMT estimate)
as part of the mitigation plan. Subsequently, the project could be required to provide annual reporting of
driveway counts collected by an acceptable third party to demonstrate the effectiveness of the adopted
mitigation measures.

Transportation Projects
Depending on the specific nature of a transportation project, it can alter trip patterns, trip lengths, and
even trip generation. Research has determined that capacity-enhancing projects can and often do increase
VMT. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as “induced demand”. While methods are generally less
developed for the analysis of induced demand compared to other areas of transportation analysis, there is
still the need to quantify and understand its impact to the transportation system considering the
requirements of SB 743.
Similar to land use projects, the approach to transportation project analysis closely aligns with the 2018
OPR Guidance. In terms of analysis, the analyst should first determine whether the transportation project
has been prescreened and determined to have a non-significant impact as described in the following
section.

Screen for Non-Significant Transportation Impact
The following non-significant impact examples are provided directly from the 2018 OPR Guidance17:
  ▪  Rehabilitation, maintenance, replacement, safety, and repair projects designed to improve the
  condition of existing transportation assets (e.g., highways, roadways, bridges, culverts);
  ▪  Transportation Management System field elements such as cameras, message signs, detection, or
  signals; tunnels; transit systems; and assets that serve bicycle and pedestrian facilities) and that do
  not add additional motor vehicle capacity;
  ▪  Roadside safety devices or hardware installation such as median barriers and guardrails;
  ▪  Roadway shoulder enhancements to provide “breakdown space,” dedicated space for use only by
  transit vehicles, to provide bicycle access, or to otherwise improve safety, but which will not be
  used as automobile vehicle travel lanes;
  ▪  Addition of an auxiliary lane of less than one mile in length designed to improve roadway safety;
  ▪  Installation, removal, or reconfiguration of traffic lanes that are not for through traffic, such as left,
  right, and U-turn pockets, two-way left turn lanes, or emergency breakdown lanes that are not
  utilized as through lanes;
  ▪  Addition of roadway capacity on local or collector streets provided the project also substantially
  improves conditions for pedestrians, cyclists, and, if applicable, transit;
  ▪  Conversion of existing general-purpose lanes (including ramps) to managed lanes or transit lanes,
  or changing lane management in a manner that would not substantially increase vehicle travel;
  ▪  Addition of a new lane that is permanently restricted to use only by transit vehicles;
  ▪  Reduction in number of through lanes;
  ▪  Grade separation to separate vehicles from rail, transit, pedestrians or bicycles, or to replace a lane
  in order to separate preferential vehicles (e.g., HOV, HOT, or trucks) from general vehicles;
  ▪  Installation, removal, or reconfiguration of traffic control devices, including Transit Signal Priority
  (TSP) features;

Significance Threshold and Methodology
For projects that increase roadway capacity and are not identified under the Non-Significant Screening
Criteria in the prior section, the significance criterion should be “Net Change” in regional VMT. A finding of
a significant impact would be determined if a transportation project results in a net increase in regional
VMT using the City’s General Plan travel demand model.

VMT Mitigation Banking Program
This section discusses a programmatic approach to respond to the need for feasible VMT mitigation within
the City of Palmdale. In suburban areas such as the City of Palmdale, VMT impact analyses can result in a
finding of a significant adverse transportation impact, particularly in undeveloped areas, due to a lack of
land use density and diversity. In addition, with fewer transportation options compared to more urbanized
areas, mitigating impacts in suburban areas can prove to be more difficult than under the former LOS
methodology for analyzing traffic impacts. For many jurisdictions like the City of Palmdale, the switch to

  12
   SB 743 VMT Implementation Guidelines for the City of Palmdale

the VMT methodology under SB 743 is resulting in a reversal in the results of transportation impact
significance findings as compared to the analyses conducted under the former LOS-based methodology.
As a practical matter, the new VMT methodology is also a more restrictive approach to identifying
transportation impacts both because of the basis for setting an impact threshold and limited mitigation
opportunities. In terms of the threshold of significance, OPR recommends that projects consisting of
residential or general employment category land uses effectively need to be located in an area where they
are 15-percent less than the regional average VMT18 for similar uses. Effectively this means that new
projects must be located in an area where they are more efficient than 65-percent of similar uses from a
VMT standpoint. Given that most development in the City of Palmdale and elsewhere is still not planned as
infill, this is resulting in an increasing need for additional feasible mitigation solutions for VMT impacts.
To date, VMT mitigation across the State has relied heavily on TDMs. These measures generally represent
two basic approaches: infrastructure and policy. The documents produced by CAPCOA regarding
mitigation, as noted previously, are some of the primary bases for estimating the effect of TDM mitigation
in California. Although CAPCOA is an invaluable resource, many of the TDM mitigation options provided
have less efficacy in suburban and rural contexts. TDMs can also be challenging from the standpoint of
mitigation monitoring and are often unpopular with project applicants because they may need to be
managed and paid for in perpetuity. These limitations have led jurisdictions, including the City of Palmdale,
to increasingly consider programmatic approaches, in addition to TDMs, for VMT mitigation. Programmatic
approaches can allow for collectively funding larger mitigation projects such that a land use or
transportation project can obtain an amount of mitigation commensurate with their impact with a single
monetary payment. Programmatic approaches can also provide a public benefit in terms of funding
transportation improvements that would not otherwise be constructed, resulting in improvements to
congestion, GHG emissions, increased transportation choices, and additional opportunities for active
transportation.
The City of Palmdale has developed a VMT Mitigation Banking Program to help address the need for VMT
mitigation. A mitigation bank attempts to create a monetary value for VMT reduction such that a developer
could purchase VMT reduction credits. These credits are then purchased for the purposes of mitigating
VMT in excess of determined impact thresholds. The underlying projects may be either regionally or locally
beneficial to the area in which the project is located.

Feasible Mitigation
This section discusses how CEQA, and the State of California, treat cases in which a project has a significant
transportation impact and therefore is required to provide feasible mitigation. Site-specific solutions often
rely on TDMs, as discussed in the previous section, although project land use modifications can also be
utilized to mitigate impacts. Projects that cannot mitigate their VMT impact fully using TDMs must rely on
non-site-specific approaches if full mitigation is to be achieved. If full mitigation is not possible, CEQA
nonetheless requires that feasible mitigation measures be imposed to reduce the severity of the impact
even if the impact remains significant with the mitigation.
Based on this, if a project cannot fully mitigate its VMT impact by implementing TDMs, it will require a
combination of site-specific measures and non-site-specific measures, including the VMT mitigation bank
discussed in the next section, in order to achieve mitigation. This could mean using only site-specific
mitigation measures to the City’s threshold, using only the VMT mitigation bank to reach the City’s
threshold, or using a combination of both site-specific mitigation measures and the VMT mitigation bank

Maximum VMT Banking Credit Rate and Nexus
The four steps to identify the VMT Mitigation Banking projects and calculate the VMT Banking credit rate
are as follows:

  1.  Identify appropriate mitigation projects
  2.  Determine the cost of construction of the mitigation projects
  3.  Determine the total VMT that can be mitigated by the projects
  4.  Calculate the maximum mitigation credit rate per VMT by dividing total cost of the mitigation
  projects by the total VMT mitigated by the projects to determine the rate per unit of VMT

The approach outlined above results in a calculation of the maximum rate per VMT mitigated based on the
list of projects identified in Exhibit 6. The full cost of funding these improvements is used to calculate the
maximum VMT Mitigation Banking credit rate per VMT the City could apply to all new residential and non-
residential development in the City that result in VMT impacts.

As part of this analysis, a nexus evaluation was undertaken to support the basis of the VMT Mitigation
Bank’s development and credit rate. Consistent with California’s Mitigation Fee Act, to develop a fee
program a local agency must identify the purpose of the fee (Section 66001(a)(1)). The City of Palmdale’s
policy is that new development shall only contribute to the VMT banking credit rate if needed for mitigation
of their VMT impacts. In addition, the costs of constructing the improvements to help mitigate VMT
citywide will be implemented through the VMT mitigation banking program administered by the City of
Palmdale.
As noted above, the projects that are included in the City of Palmdale’s VMT Mitigation Banking Program
will fund the construction of facilities that support active transportation (cycling) to mitigate VMT impacts
from new development by moving trips from automobiles to bike facilities. As the benefit provided by the
VMT reducing projects could not be sufficiently analyzed using the City’s General Plan travel demand model
given limitations within the model related to the representation of bike facilities, the projects were
analyzed using off-model techniques. Specifically, bicycle improvements were evaluated based on NCHRP
552 Guidelines for Analysis of Investments in Bicycle Facilities. This approach relies on spatial analysis
techniques to determine the likely number of new active transportation users resulting from the
introduction of a new bicycle facility. This approach also removes the number of new users who will use
the facility for exercise as exercise will not replace vehicle trips and thus, will not reduce existing VMT.
Based on survey data of bicyclists throughout the United States, both for adults and children, the
percentage of those cycling for commute purposes was estimated to be 11-percent of all riders and those
cycling for exercise was estimated to be 28-percent of all riders. Child cyclists are included in the analysis
as they may use the new facility to access schools, friends, or stores among other destinations that
previously they would need a parent to drive them to. Thus, with the removal of riders for exercise, only
riders that would use the facilities to replace vehicle trips were included in the analysis. Exhibit 7 shows the
comparison between the existing ridership and future induced riders based on the construction of the
projects.

As shown in Exhibit 7, the VMT-reducing projects could add almost 10,480 bicycle trips per day throughout
the City by 2033. The replacement of vehicle trips by the induced riders will provide an alternative to

should also be noted that construction of the pedestrian and bicycle improvements will result in additional
safety benefits by reducing the potential for vehicle-bicycle and vehicle-pedestrian conflicts.
The park and ride facility at 10th Street West (Project #38) was examined for its VMT reduction capabilities
as part of the Palmdale Park and Ride Study. The total market for the new park and ride was calculated
based on the service area taken from existing facilities, capture of the existing carpool market due to added
convenience of additional park and ride facilities, and the ability to transfer to transit routes that serve
stops near the park and ride. The total reduction of VMT from the opening of the proposed location at 10th
Street West is 1,378,627 VMT travelled per year or roughly 3,777 VMT per day. For more information on
the methodology and the calculations, see the Palmdale Park and Ride Study dated March 2024.

Total VMT Reduction
The total VMT reduction per project for the bicycle projects was calculated by multiplying the average
bicycle trip length taken by new riders induced by the construction of a project by the total number of new
riders and the project’s lifecycle. For the purposes of this analysis, the average bicycle trip length used was
1.8-miles, based on data from the Replica transportation analytics platform. The number of new bicycle
riders for each project was multiplied by the average trip length to obtain the total daily VMT reduction for
each project. Each project’s VMT reduction was added together to determine the total VMT reduction for
all bicycle projects, which for the projects listed in Exhibit 6 total 18,860 daily VMT.

VMT Banking Credit Rate
To determine the overall VMT banking credit rate, the total project costs of for the bicycle and park and
ride lot projects were estimated as $2,910,917 and $3,000,000, respectively, for a total project cost of
$5,910,917. This cost was divided by the total VMT reductions for the bicycle and park and ride projects,
which are 18,860 and 3,777 daily VMT, respectively, for a total daily VMT reduction of 22,637 VMT. This
calculation resulted in a cost per VMT reduction of $261. Note that this rate does not include any non-fee
funding sources (grants, etc.). The addition of any funding sources for these projects could reduce the cost
to fully implement projects included in Exhibit 6.
Note that the VMT Banking Credit Rate provided above will be updated on an ongoing basis in response to
changes to the program, underlying projects, and/or updated cost information. As such, the VMT banking
credit rate provided above should not be assumed to represent the current rate and instead that should be
obtained directly from the City’s website.

VMT Mitigation Banking Program Administration and Monitoring
The City of Palmdale shall set up a separate account for the purpose of tracking the collection of payments
into the VMT Mitigation Banking Program and the VMT Analysis Fee to run and maintain the TREDLite
analysis tool. The fee for the City of Palmdale to run TREDLite for new projects is $600. These accounts shall
be monitored by the City Engineer or person designated by the City Engineer to ensure purchased VMT
credits are used for constructing appropriate projects, as identified in Exhibit 6, to achieve the intended
VMT reduction. As part of the annual city budget process, the City Engineer, Public Works Director, or
person designated by either of these individuals shall include a progress report on any funds accumulated
in the VMT Mitigation Banking Program and expenditures on constructing or improving active
transportation facilities providing additional VMT-reducing investments that would not have occurred if
bank funding were not available.

Substantial Evidence for Unit-Based Screening Thresholds for Small Projects
This document identifies a 3,000 Metric Tons of Carbon Dioxide Equivalent (MTCO2e) per year screening
level threshold to identify projects that require the use of the screening tables or a project-specific technical
analysis to quantify and mitigate project emissions. Projects that generate less than 3,000 Metric Tons (MT)
of "Carbon Dioxide Equivalent (CO2e)" per year can be presumed to have less than significant impact on
VMT since the intent and goals of SB 743 are to meet the State’s GHG reduction goals. A threshold of 3,000
MT of CO2e per year is consistent with the CEQA GHG threshold of significance recommended by the South
Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), which is the most stringent in the region. Several recent
CEQA documents produced for development projects within the City of Palmdale use the 3,000 MTCO2e
threshold including the Palmdale Logistics Park EIR and the 8th Street Industrial EIR.

The City of Palmdale determined the size of development that is too small to be able to provide the level
of greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions expected from the screening tables or alternate emission
analysis method. To do this the City determined the GHG emission amount allowed by a project such that
90-percent of the emissions, on average, from all projects would exceed that level and be “captured” by
the screening table or alternate emission analysis method. The GHG emissions calculations from the City’s
VMT Analysis Tool should be used in conjunction with the City’s GHG emissions screening tables.
California Emissions Estimator Model (CalEEMod 2022.1) was used to determine the maximum number of
dwelling units or square footage that would remain within the 3,000 MTCO2e per year screening threshold.
CalEEMod is a statewide land use emissions computer model designed to quantify potential criteria
pollutant emissions associated with both construction and operations from a variety of land use projects.
This model was selected because it is provided by the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to be used
statewide for developing project‐level GHG emissions. CalEEMod was used with the built‐in default trip
lengths and types.
CalEEMod runs were conducted for a variety of land uses in order to determine the land use units that
trigger the 3,000 MT CO2e/year threshold, as well the CO2e emissions on a per-unit (dwelling unit or
thousand square feet) rate that could be used in the City’s VMT Analysis Tool. The land uses and
corresponding CO2e emissions rates are shown in Table B-1.

DISCUSSION

A density bonus is an increase in the overall number of housing units that a developer
may build on a site in exchange for providing affordable housing. State Density Bonus
Law, pursuant to Section 65915 of the California Government Code, offers incentives that
are intended to encourage the development of affordable housing, including up to an 80
percent increase in density.

The project site has a General Plan Land Use designation and zone of Single-Family
Residential 3 (SFR 3, 7,000 square foot lots; up to six dwelling units per acre). The project
site is approximately 20 acres, and the maximum density is 120 detached single-family
residential units. Density Bonus Law requires that when 10 percent of all units are for low-
income households, the City must grant a 20 percent density bonus over the base density,
which would allow an additional four units for this development. Although the maximum
density for the project site is 120 units, the residential development does not require an
increased density and the applicant proposes to construct a total of 64 detached single-
family residential units and 127 ADU’s and JADU’s for a total of 191 residential units.
Under California Fair Housing Laws, the proposed ADUs and JADUs are not subject to a
jurisdiction's density requirements.

Of the 191 units proposed, 10 percent of the units are required to be reserved for low-
income households. Additionally, the owner has requested cost-saving concessions in
accordance with Government Code Section 65915, et seq. and PMC Section 17.25.020
(Density Bonus Agreements), as follows:

  1.  To allow composite shingles for roofing material.

  2.  To allow a reduction of the required garage width of 20 feet.

The Housing Division has determined that granting the concessions listed above will
result in actual and identifiable cost reductions to provide affordable housing. In addition,
the proposed project will contribute to the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment
(RHNA) allocation.

  RECITALS

  A.  The Owner is the owner of a fee interest in certain real property located in the City
of Palmdale, County of Los Angeles, State of California, identified as APN 3023-002-184, located
at the Southeast corner of East Palmdale Boulevard and Hudsonia Street and legally described in
Exhibit “A” attached hereto and incorporated by reference (the “Property”).

  B.  The Owner will construct a 191-unit affordable housing development, 64 three- and
four-bedroom single family homes, 64 one-bedroom junior accessory dwelling units, 48 two-
bedroom accessory dwelling units (“ADUs”), 15 three-bedroom ADUs, and associated
landscaping and parking (“Residential Development” of “Project”).

  C.  The Owner proposes construction of a rental housing development of 189 units for
low-income individuals and families and two manager’s unit. At least ten percent (10%) of the
units that count towards the Project’s base density as defined pursuant to Government Code section
65915 (64 units) will be available to and occupied by households whose incomes do not exceed
the maximum income of low-income households in Los Angeles County as determined by the
California Department of Housing and Community Development.
 Density Bonus Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-8767
Maison’s Palmdale Blvd 150, LLC  Page 2
APN: 3023-002-184

  D.  Under California Government Code Section 65915, et seq. and Palmdale Municipal
Code Section 17.25.020, the City must, upon the request of an applicant, grant a density bonus
and/or certain incentives/concessions and/or waivers/modifications for any development applicant
that seeks and agrees to construct a minimum number of housing units that are affordable to low
or very low-income households (the “Density Bonus Law”).

  E.  The subject site has a General Plan Land Use Designation of Single Family
Residential 3 (up to 6 dwelling units per acre) and is zoned Single Family Residential 3 (up to 6
dwelling units per acre). The Density Bonus Law requires that, when an applicant includes at least
10% low-income units, the City must grant a 20% density bonus over the base density, which
would allow an additional 4 units per acre in the Residential Development. Because ADUs do not
count towards density, the Project does not require a density bonus. To provide for affordable
housing cost of the low-income units and fit the Project on the Property as designed, the Owner
has requested a cost-saving concession and a waiver in accordance with California Government
Code Section 65915, et seq. and Palmdale Municipal Code Section 17.25.020, as follows:

  a.  A concession pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Section 17.37.010.D.7,
  to allow composite shingles for the roofing material.

  F.  The Owner has also requested one waiver to development standards that, if applied,
would have the effect of physically precluding the construction of the Project in accordance with
California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (e)(1), as follows:

  a.  A waiver to the minimum garage length in Palmdale Municipal Code
  Section 17.37.010.C.3.b to allow a minimum garage length of 20 feet.

  G.  The City and the Owner enter into this Agreement pursuant to and in accordance
with California Government Code Section 65915, et seq., and Section 17.25.020 of the Palmdale
Municipal Code, in order to provide housing for lower income households.

  H.  The City finds that granting the concession and waiver listed under Recital E and
F, above, will result in actual and identifiable cost reductions to provide for affordable housing
cost, will not have an adverse impact upon public health and safety, the physical environment, or
any property that is listed in the California Register of Historical Resources, and is consistent with
state and federal law. The City also finds that the Residential Development is consistent with the
General Plan.

RECOMMENDATION

Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-018, approving the Five-Year Public Art Work Plan in
accordance with Chapter 15.01 of the Palmdale Municipal Code.

BACKGROUND

The City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2020-084, approving the Public Art Master
Plan (Master Plan) and directed staff to implement the Master Plan’s recommendations
diligently. Consistent with this direction, the Public Art Commission and staff developed
an annual Five-Year Public Art Work Plan (Five-Year Plan) that charts current and future
public art projects and determines resources and funding priorities. The Five-Year Plan
strategy is updated annually to include City-funded projects, public/private partnerships,
maintenance, and a conservation plan. The City Council approves the proposed Five-
Year Plan as part of the City’s annual budget adoption process.

DISCUSSION

The Five-Year Plan sets the course for implementing all municipal public art projects,
including the artwork's scope, concept, location, budget, and timeline. The preliminary
Public Art Fund balance as of June 30, 2023, is $1,491,630. Most of these funds were
allocated from the City’s General Fund to initiate the program.

The Public Art Commission reviewed the draft Five-Year Plan at their January 23, 2024,
meeting, and the final form was reviewed and discussed at their March 26, 2024, meeting.
After discussion, the commission adopted Resolution No. PAC 2024-002, recommending
the Five-Year Plan for City Council approval in accordance with Chapter 15.01 of the

   COMMUNITY OUTREACH

The community engagement process in public art helps to develop criteria for artist selection, the artwork
character and location, and provides background information on the project that informs the artist’s
scope of work. In the Public Art Master Plan, the top four responses from the public art community
survey What Makes Palmdale Unique are:

•  Diversity (Cultures, Friendly People, Community, Multi-Cultural);
•  Landscape (Desert, Joshua Trees, Yucca Trees, Poppies, Lake);
•  Aerospace (History, Military, Northrop, Lockheed); and
•  Views (Mountains, Sunsets, Sunrises, Stars, Foothills, Blue Skies).

In addition to the themes above, residents are asked to reflect on the property and its impact on the
surrounding neighborhood. These topics have been included in our recent public art surveys (English
and Spanish). Community outreach for public art projects has been conducted via our online survey
portal, available through the City’s social media platforms, the monthly newsletter, City-owned facilities,
neighborhood watch captains, Partners Against Crime apartment managers, on-site signage and project
QR code, and at several City programs hosted at the Palmdale Amphitheater and the Palmdale
Playhouse. The results of our 2023 outreach efforts indicates that people identifying as Latino completed
the largest number of surveys, averaging at 36%, with people identifying as White following closely at
31%.

BACKGROUND

On July 1, 2018, the City entered into a Franchise Agreement with Waste Management
of Antelope Valley (WM) for Integrated Solid Waste Management services for residents
and commercial properties. On September 1, 2019, the City Council approved the First
Amendment of the Agreement to clarify language omitted by the then procurement
consultant and to prepare for changes in solid waste regulations.

The City of Palmdale continues to work on compliance with the requirements of Senate
Bill 1383 (SB 1383). This law was voted in place in 2016 with various requirements
including the implementation of an organics recycling program.

DISCUSSION

Under the new proposed scope of services, the following updates have been negotiated
and are before you for consideration:

    Ten (10) year agreement term extension, making the new expiration date June
  30, 2036;
    One-time adjustment to rates commencing on July 1, 2024. The current Standard
  Service Rate (FY23/24) of $35.08 will increase to an Estimated Standard Service
  Rate (FY24/25) of $40.22. This increase includes both the regular annual
  adjustment outlined in the existing agreement and the negotiated increase;
    Memorialize actual curb miles swept (2,268) from existing (1,505) to account for
  City growth;
    Increase curb mile rate to align with market rates and better prepare for upcoming
  changes in law;
    Regular street sweeping performance meetings;
    Consolidates the Biennial Audit fee; and,
    Consolidates the SB1383 Support fee.

The following City benefits were negotiated:

    $8.5M Franchise Extension Fee upon execution of the amendment;
    $100K for cameras to capture illegal dumping activity purchased directly by WM
  upon execution of the amendment at the direction of the City;
    Franchise Fee adjustment from 14.3% to 17.0%; and,
    To incentivize participation and minimize illegal dumping, simplify and rebalance
  roll off rates starting July 1, 2024, including a decrease in rates for most utilized
  sizes (40 yds & 50 yds bins):

The proposed updates to the scope of services present a comprehensive and balanced
approach consistent with industry standards and direction. The negotiated changes
extend the Agreement term, align rates with neighboring jurisdictions, and improve
accountability through performance meetings while adjusting certain fees.

Additionally, the City stands to gain significant benefits, including investments in
surveillance technology and adjustments to franchise fees. Moreover, the proposed
simplification and rebalancing of roll-off rates aim to provide more equitable pricing for
services. Overall, these updates reflect a collaborative effort to enhance service delivery
in accordance with current industry practices, addressing the impact of new state
regulations and providing funding for state-mandated programs. All remaining contract
items not specifically outlined in this amendment, remain in full force and effect.

SUBJECT:  STAFF FOLLOW-UP RESPONSE TO APRIL 3, 2024, CITY COUNCIL
  DIRECTION: DISCUSSION ON OPTIONS FOR LANGUAGE
  INTERPRETATION SERVICES AT COUNCIL MEETINGS

RECOMMENDATION

Adopt the use of City Staff as interpreters while further investigation into software
services is being carried out.

BACKGROUND

At the April 3, 2024, meeting, the Council directed staff to bring back a report on potential
options for providing language interpretation services at council meetings.

DISCUSSION

City staff is exploring the possible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions and providing
interpreting services through our certified Spanish-speaking employees.

The City has a number of certified employees who provide Spanish interpretation
assistance to residents and customers. The employees will be polled to see who is
available to interpret at the meetings.

The Information Technology Division is reviewing several Artificial Intelligence (AI)
platforms for security and compatibility.

For efficiency and cost containment, we are not recommending third-party translation
services at this time.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; there is no fiscal impact associated with this action.
